radiate

RAY-dee-ayt -- from Latin radius, 'ray': a feeling comes off you like rays from a source. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To radiate is to give off a feeling or quality you genuinely have, so clearly that no one can miss it.

The grandmother seemed to radiate warmth the moment she stepped into a room full of strangers.

Example

A candidate walks onstage in front of a hostile crowd and, without raising his voice or hurrying a single word, radiates a calm that leaves the whole hall convinced he is not the least bit worried.

His calm fills the hall without ever being stated -- that is radiating a feeling. Unlike 'announce,' which needs words, radiating happens through presence alone.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

project: To project is to send an impression outward on purpose, the way an actor fills a theater with a character's feelings. To radiate is to give off a feeling you genuinely have; there is no performance in it. What you project may be an act; what you radiate is real.

beam: To beam is to show happiness in a glowing smile -- it lives on the face, and it is almost always joy. To radiate is bigger: a person radiates warmth, calm, or menace through their whole presence, so clearly that no one nearby can miss it.

convey: To convey is to get a feeling or idea across to someone -- one message, delivered by words, looks, or gestures. To radiate is steady and automatic: you give off a feeling you genuinely have, and everyone around you picks it up without your trying.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

conceal: to keep something from being seen

suppress: to hold a feeling down and keep it in

Where it sits · how steadily the feeling pours out

show → radiate → exude

show vs. radiate: Show is the plain, everyday version of radiate -- you can show annoyance with one frown, while to radiate a feeling is to give it off so steadily that everyone nearby senses it.

exude vs. radiate: Exude is even more insistent than radiate: to radiate confidence is to give it off clearly, while to exude confidence suggests it seeps out of a person constantly, whether they mean it to or not.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — radi-: ray, beam, spoke of a wheel (Latin (radius))

suffix — -ate: verb-forming ending: to do or make (Latin (-atus))

Put it together: Latin radiare meant 'to shine out in rays,' from radius, the spoke of a wheel or a beam of light -- when someone radiates confidence, the feeling spreads outward from them like spokes from a hub, the same root behind radius and radio.

Use the root in a new word: radius: The quiz asks you to find each circle's radius before anything else.

Root Check

Word Choice

Radiate has a literal sense (heat and light radiate from a fire), but on the ISEE it usually appears in its figurative sense: a person radiates joy, calm, menace, or confidence. This unit teaches only that figurative sense.
